evidence.title: Stenting for a Ruptured Blood Blister-Like Aneurysm of the Basilar Artery: Case Report and Literature Review.
evidence.abstract: Blood blister-like aneurysms (BBAs) usually occur on the supraclinoid portion of the internal carotid artery. There are a few reports of BBAs in other locations. We provide the case details of a ruptured BBA of the basilar artery (BA) that was treated with stenting, with a good outcome. The patient was a 74-year-old Japanese woman with a World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade I subarachnoid hemorrhage. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) performed on day 14 revealed a BBA with a maximum diameter of 1.5 mm and a wide neck on the posterior wall of the BA's tip. Single stenting was performed on day 20, and an additional stenting was performed on day 26 due to postoperative stent migration. At six months post-operation, DSA revealed that the aneurysm had disappeared, and the patient was recovering well. Ruptured BBAs of the BA are rare and difficult to treat due to high rates of rebleeding and the presence of significant perforating branches. BBAs located on the posterior wall, in particular, are at high risk of ischemic complications. If coil embolization within an aneurysm is difficult, stenting alone may also be an effective treatment.

evidence.title: Combined Pipeline Embolization and Coiling of an Intracranial Aneurysm in Marfan Syndrome: A Case Report and Literature Review.
evidence.abstract: Background and importance Marfan syndrome's association with intracranial aneurysms, though controversial, poses unique challenges for surgical intervention because of the inherent vascular fragility. Open surgical approaches carry considerable risk. Endovascular flow diversion with the Pipeline embolization device (PED) offers a less invasive alternative, and adjunctive coiling can decrease occlusion time for complex aneurysms. We report the first combined use of PED and coiling to treat a Marfan-associated intracranial aneurysm, detailing our operative approach and reviewing the literature. Clinical presentation A 53-year-old patient with a pathological FBN1 mutation was incidentally found to have an unruptured paraophthalmic aneurysm during stroke workup. Diagnostic angiography revealed an irregular superior hypophyseal aneurysm along with tortuous and irregular internal carotid arteries suggesting previous dissections. The aneurysm was successfully treated with a PED and adjunctive coil embolization. The patient was discharged on aspirin and clopidogrel. Six-month follow-up angiography confirmed aneurysm occlusion. Although there was no residual or recurrent aneurysm at 2-year follow-up, imaging revealed 2 de novo intracranial aneurysms. The patient remains asymptomatic and under observation. Conclusion This is the first case of combined PED and coiling for an intracranial aneurysm in Marfan syndrome. This dual approach may offer safer and more effective treatment than traditional methods. In addition, the formation of de novo aneurysms underscores the importance of long-term angiographic follow-up in patients with FBN1 mutations to monitor for evolving vascular pathology. These findings warrant further investigation into identifying a genetic link between FBN1 mutations and cerebrovascular pathology.

evidence.title: Comaneci stent-angioplasty for the optimization of inadequately deployed flow diverter stents.
evidence.abstract: Background and PurposeIn endovascular procedures, inadequate deployment of a flow diverter stent is a highly concerning technical complication that can lead to acute parent vessel occlusion and ischaemic events. This study aimed to assess the off-label use of the Comaneci device in managing technical difficulties associated with flow diversion.Materials and MethodsWe conducted an analysis of all flow diverter procedures documented in our prospectively collected database. Our objective was to identify patients with inadequately deployed implants who underwent Comaneci stent-angioplasty. Both Comaneci 17 and Comaneci 21 devices were utilized to address and remediate technical complications related to stent deployment. We reviewed anatomical features, technical details, intraprocedural complications, as well as clinical and angiographic outcomes.ResultsThirty-one Comaneci devices were employed to remediate 31 inadequately deployed flow diverter stents. Successful resolution of technical complications associated with flow diverter placement was achieved in all attempted cases. No clinically significant complications were attributed to the technique, and no mortality was observed during the study.ConclusionTechnical issues arising from flow diverter stent deployment are formidable complications. Familiarity with appropriate corrective manoeuvres is essential to achieve successful outcomes. The Comaneci device can be safely and effectively incorporated into the range of techniques used to rectify inadequately deployed stents.

evidence.title: Flow diversion of cerebral aneurysms in Type I osteogenesis imperfecta: A case report of the first two treatments in humans.
evidence.abstract: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) predisposes individuals to easy bone fracture, vessel fragility, and platelet dysfunction. We report the first known case of neurointerventional treatment with flow diversion of intracranial aneurysms in a patient with OI. A 62 year-old female with known OI Type I, history of >40 lifetime bone fractures and hypertension, underwent workup for transient ischemic attacks revealing a 4-mm right A1 segment aneurysm in 2016. Perioperative dual antiplatelet therapy was aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 37.5 mg daily. Tri-axial access was utilized to deploy a 3.5 × 16-mm Pipeline Flex device without complication. Two-month follow-up revealed Raymond I (O'Kelly Marotta I) obliteration of the aneurysm. Five-year follow-up revealed a de novo left-sided 3-mm A1-A2 junction aneurysm. A 4 × 12-mm Surpass Evolve was placed without complication. Six-month follow-up revealed Raymond I (O'Kelly Marotta I) obliteration of the second aneurysm. The patient remained asymptomatic at all follow-up visits.

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Blood blister-like aneurysms (BBAs) usually occur on the supraclinoid portion of the internal carotid artery. There are a few reports of BBAs in other locations. We provide the case details of a ruptured BBA of the basilar artery (BA) that was treated with stenting, with a good outcome. The patient was a 74-year-old Japanese woman with a World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade I subarachnoid hemorrhage. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) performed on day 14 revealed a BBA with a maximum diameter of 1.5 mm and a wide neck on the posterior wall of the BA's tip. Single stenting was performed on day 20, and an additional stenting was performed on day 26 due to postoperative stent migration. At six months post-operation, DSA revealed that the aneurysm had disappeared, and the patient was recovering well. Ruptured BBAs of the BA are rare and difficult to treat due to high rates of rebleeding and the presence of significant perforating branches. BBAs located on the posterior wall, in particular, are at high risk of ischemic complications. If coil embolization within an aneurysm is difficult, stenting alone may also be an effective treatment.

custody_records.raw_content: Background and importance Marfan syndrome's association with intracranial aneurysms, though controversial, poses unique challenges for surgical intervention because of the inherent vascular fragility. Open surgical approaches carry considerable risk. Endovascular flow diversion with the Pipeline embolization device (PED) offers a less invasive alternative, and adjunctive coiling can decrease occlusion time for complex aneurysms. We report the first combined use of PED and coiling to treat a Marfan-associated intracranial aneurysm, detailing our operative approach and reviewing the literature. Clinical presentation A 53-year-old patient with a pathological FBN1 mutation was incidentally found to have an unruptured paraophthalmic aneurysm during stroke workup. Diagnostic angiography revealed an irregular superior hypophyseal aneurysm along with tortuous and irregular internal carotid arteries suggesting previous dissections. The aneurysm was successfully treated with a PED and adjunctive coil embolization. The patient was discharged on aspirin and clopidogrel. Six-month follow-up angiography confirmed aneurysm occlusion. Although there was no residual or recurrent aneurysm at 2-year follow-up, imaging revealed 2 de novo intracranial aneurysms. The patient remains asymptomatic and under observation. Conclusion This is the first case of combined PED and coiling for an intracranial aneurysm in Marfan syndrome. This dual approach may offer safer and more effective treatment than traditional methods. In addition, the formation of de novo aneurysms underscores the importance of long-term angiographic follow-up in patients with FBN1 mutations to monitor for evolving vascular pathology. These findings warrant further investigation into identifying a genetic link between FBN1 mutations and cerebrovascular pathology.

custody_records.raw_content: Background and PurposeIn endovascular procedures, inadequate deployment of a flow diverter stent is a highly concerning technical complication that can lead to acute parent vessel occlusion and ischaemic events. This study aimed to assess the off-label use of the Comaneci device in managing technical difficulties associated with flow diversion.Materials and MethodsWe conducted an analysis of all flow diverter procedures documented in our prospectively collected database. Our objective was to identify patients with inadequately deployed implants who underwent Comaneci stent-angioplasty. Both Comaneci 17 and Comaneci 21 devices were utilized to address and remediate technical complications related to stent deployment. We reviewed anatomical features, technical details, intraprocedural complications, as well as clinical and angiographic outcomes.ResultsThirty-one Comaneci devices were employed to remediate 31 inadequately deployed flow diverter stents. Successful resolution of technical complications associated with flow diverter placement was achieved in all attempted cases. No clinically significant complications were attributed to the technique, and no mortality was observed during the study.ConclusionTechnical issues arising from flow diverter stent deployment are formidable complications. Familiarity with appropriate corrective manoeuvres is essential to achieve successful outcomes. The Comaneci device can be safely and effectively incorporated into the range of techniques used to rectify inadequately deployed stents.

custody_records.raw_content: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) predisposes individuals to easy bone fracture, vessel fragility, and platelet dysfunction. We report the first known case of neurointerventional treatment with flow diversion of intracranial aneurysms in a patient with OI. A 62 year-old female with known OI Type I, history of >40 lifetime bone fractures and hypertension, underwent workup for transient ischemic attacks revealing a 4-mm right A1 segment aneurysm in 2016. Perioperative dual antiplatelet therapy was aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 37.5 mg daily. Tri-axial access was utilized to deploy a 3.5 × 16-mm Pipeline Flex device without complication. Two-month follow-up revealed Raymond I (O'Kelly Marotta I) obliteration of the aneurysm. Five-year follow-up revealed a de novo left-sided 3-mm A1-A2 junction aneurysm. A 4 × 12-mm Surpass Evolve was placed without complication. Six-month follow-up revealed Raymond I (O'Kelly Marotta I) obliteration of the second aneurysm. The patient remained asymptomatic at all follow-up visits.
